rewrites.summary:
The capital's courts have been the country's clearest rights forum for trans people: a ruling finalised in July 2024 held that police who told a transgender person mid-legal-transition to avoid public restrooms for a while had infringed personal rights, calling comfortable restroom use a fundamental and universal human right and awarding damages. A 2021 district-court judgment likewise awarded damages against a beauty academy that barred a trans student's restroom use.

Practical safety rests in part on national data a visitor shares in public facilities: a 2021 survey of 591 trans respondents found 41% had used a restroom of another gender out of fear of mistreatment, 39% restricted food and drink to avoid public restrooms, and 36% went without. On recognition and documents, gender-marker change has liberalised judicially: a May 2024 regional decision approved marker change for five trans people without surgery, holding that a surgery requirement violates bodily integrity and reducing the old surgical prerequisites to reference-only status, though some courts still apply them.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: National-framework context colours the visit without being capital-specific: the 2021 survey data is country-wide evidence, and the May 2024 gender-marker approval issued from a regional court outside the capital, reflecting a national judicial trend in which some courts still apply the older surgical prerequisites.
rewrites.localsOnly: School facilities are resident/student-facing: binary school restrooms leave 69% of trans students surveyed (86 respondents) uncomfortable, with documented patterns of avoiding water and leaving school early to avoid outing, and a regional study (208 respondents) reported 39% mistreatment; legislative advocacy for gender-neutral single-occupant restrooms and inclusive school rules concerns the domestic school system, which foreign visitors do not enter.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: No source addresses border-screening or document-recognition practice for trans visitors to the capital, and no marriage or partner-travel information is recorded. The survey figures are self-reported, and the reported judicial protections do not establish that day-to-day police conduct outside those cases is consistent.

rewrites.summary:
Worse than national for what a visitor actually meets: this is the main tourist corridor, a large international tourism envelope with a commercially gay-friendly surface, but police forces at both municipal and state level have repeatedly been documented committing discriminatory acts against LGBT+ people. Multiple recorded assaults during detention are concentrated in the two most visited resort towns; officers are described as untrained in human-rights standards; the municipal diversity office recorded three formal discrimination complaints in a single year, including violence against a transgender woman; and two tourist-police members were fired after their own body cameras showed them running an extortion ring against visitors with portable card terminals.

Documents and screening: the airport city's immigration detention facility is documented as a place of systematic rights violations with no accountability — directly relevant to a visitor whose documents are questioned. Useful legal counterweights are resident-facing, and the record is scored relative to the national score (0.55) for Mexico.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Parent-nation policy flux and the wider legal picture are adjacent: a March 2025 national assessment documented 22 of 32 states with a legal gender-recognition procedure and six states with no reform, leaving permanently mismatched documents and recording coercive detention and border-scrutiny risks for mismatched travellers nationwide; the civil code has permitted same-sex marriage since 2012 (after a 2011–2012 annulment and reinstatement episode); same-sex adoption was legalised in August 2022; the penal code sits among hate-crime laws punishing crimes motivated by sexual orientation or gender; and the elected legislature of a neighbouring state banned conversion practices in the same December 2023 reform. None of this changes a visitor's on-the-ground exposure in the tourist corridor.
rewrites.localsOnly: Quintana Roo's 2020 legal gender recognition procedure and its December 2023 ban on conversion practices are resident-facing; neither changes the exposure of a visitor.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Police-misconduct patterns are documented through complaints, recorded incidents and press coverage rather than official statistics, so true prevalence is unverified; and the sources do not say whether visitors and residents are treated differently at the immigration facility, beyond the documented systemic rights-violation pattern.

An online encyclopaedia page on LGBTQ rights in the parent nation provides the state/province-level legal picture a visitor stands under: same-sex marriage has been permitted in this state/province since 2012 (two marriages were performed in a small town in November 2011, annulled by the governor in April 2012, and reinstated on 3 May 2012 once the state/province conceded that its civil code sets no gender requirement); adoption by same-sex couples was legalised in August 2022; it ranks among the state/province units that enacted legal gender recognition in 2020 and banned conversion practices on 15 December 2023; its penal code is listed among hate-crime laws punishing crimes motivated by sexual orientation or gender; it ratified a 2011 national constitutional ban on sexual-orientation discrimination; and the main tourist airport city ranks among the nation's principal gay-tourism destinations.

rewrites.summary:
No protective or tolerant regime specific to this state is on record: a visitor's exposure is the national baseline, enforced locally. Same-sex conduct is criminalised with up to 20 years' imprisonment and whipping, there is no legal gender recognition, and public-morality offences are enforced through the state's religious authorities — the channel international monitoring documents as driving state-backed discrimination against LGBT people; state religious law separately criminalises cross-dressing and same-sex intimacy for Muslims.

The one documented local divergence beyond that baseline is adverse: in November 2023 the state government announced plans to establish 'conversion-therapy centres' to rehabilitate LGBT people.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: National enforcement context colours the local picture: a crackdown on the LGBT community has run since the 2018 election and is country-wide rather than specific to this state; the enforcement channel described in the summary is the same one international monitoring identifies nationwide.
rewrites.localsOnly: Resident-facing data: there is no legal gender recognition route for residents, and the 'rehabilitation programmes' under the national crackdown in this country had drawn more than a thousand attendees by June 2021 (1,733 at last count) — recorded evidence of the scale of resident exposure, not a fact about a visitor's passage.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Whether the November 2023 conversion-therapy-centre plans were ever put into operation is not reported. No source addresses border-screening or document-recognition practice for trans visitors to this state, and no marriage or partner-travel information is recorded.

rewrites.summary:
Worse than national: the territory's most publicly visible trans person was killed on 8 August 2024 — found beaten and bruised beside a main highway hours after posting a routine video, having previously expressed fear for her life — and police have not charged anyone. A human-rights group has sued the federal government and the police for failing to investigate, seeking a court order to compel investigation and prosecution after multiple petitions were ignored, which qualifies the killing under a test of official failure rather than leaving it a lone incident. Reporting on the capital's queer scene documents threats and raids alongside informal community organising.

The national framework applies here unchanged for a visitor: a 2014 act reinforcing colonial-era laws criminalises same-sex conduct with up to 14 years' imprisonment, extends to people who help arrange or conduct same-sex marriages and to activities of gay groups and organisations; dating-app gangs are a documented extortion pattern country-wide; and a foreign government's travel advisory (August 2026) warned LGBT travellers of arrest, violence, attacks and blackmail risks. Scored relative to the national score (0.08).
rewrites.tangentialFactors: National and regional comparisons: religious-law regions to the north can impose death by stoning for same-sex conduct, the national military bans cross-dressing, and a nearly 6,000-signature petition demanded the killing be investigated as a hate crime — adjacent national-context items that colour the climate without being capital-specific.
rewrites.localsOnly: Resident-facing practice: there is no legal route to change gender markers.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Six months after the killing no suspects had been charged despite a promised thorough and discreet investigation, and the lawsuit's outcome is unresolved; the dating-app-gang pattern is documented country-wide but not specific to this territory, and no source addresses border-screening or document-recognition practice for trans visitors to the capital.

The local police chief ordered a 'thorough and discreet' investigation, and the report notes that although national law guarantees freedom from discrimination, mass arrests and detention of LGBTQ+ people are common, especially in religious-law regions.

National-framework source (applies country-wide; no local-specific breakdown): reporting (19 August 2026) that a foreign nation's foreign office warned LGBT+ travellers of the risk of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation, advised that same-sex sexual activity is illegal and can attract lengthy prison sentences and that some regions operating under religious law can impose the death penalty, and that the law also extends to people who help arrange or conduct same-sex marriages and criminalises activities involving gay groups and organisations; breaching curfews or movement restrictions could expose travellers to arrest and detention.

rewrites.summary:
Lima concentrates the country's sharpest documented lethal risk and its newest legal restriction. A national observatory counted 54 LGBTI+ murders for 2020–2023, with trans women the most affected (30 of the dead), amid rising hate crimes in which no suspects were identified in 26 of the 54 killings.

In 2025 the national congress — sitting in the capital — approved a norm barring trans people from public bathrooms of a sex not matching their birth sex (committee vote February 2025, plenary approval April 2025), with the text also barring 'ambiguous' bathroom signage of the kind the capital's international airport had installed. A national human-rights institute analysed the norm as legalised discrimination with direct consequences for access to public space, and enforcement is expected to rest on security staff's judgment of whether an entering woman is trans. For a trans visitor, the capital is where both mechanisms bite: the bathroom-restriction norm is national policy administered here, and the murder pattern shows the violence exposure when prosecutions are rare and official statistics thin.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: National-policy attribution: the bathroom norm was enacted by the national congress that sits in the capital, binding every region equally, so this record's capital-specific weight rests on the documented violence and crime data rather than on the norm itself.
rewrites.localsOnly: Resident-facing data underlines the context: the observatory's victim counts concern residents — 54 LGBTI+ murders for 2020–2023 with trans women most affected — because official statistics do not record victims' sexual orientation; the bathroom norm also governs residents' daily access to public facilities.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
General crime is concentrated in the capital: the central district leads the national frequency of reported crimes overall (10.0%; eleven district prosecutorial areas hold 62%) — general crime and political instability affect all travellers, not trans-specific.

The observatory's murder counts rest on observatory data rather than official statistics, which do not record victims' sexual orientation, and whether the 2025 bathroom norm is being enforced in practice is not reported.

rewrites.summary:
Malta is among the safest countries in the world for transgender visitors. It has ranked first for LGBTI legal rights in its region every year since 2015: gender identity and expression are protected from discrimination in law, legal gender recognition works by self-determination, and 'X' gender markers are available on passports. Conversion therapy is banned and the constitution guarantees LGBTI equality.

Malta records one of the lowest rates of physical or sexual victimisation of LGBTIQ+ people in its region, and the national police force has adopted hate-crime procedures for sexual-orientation and gender-identity incidents. A foreign government's diplomatic guidance describes the country as a safe environment for foreign LGBT travellers, and no government travel advisory flags trans-specific concerns.

Residual risks are minor: non-physical harassment (including online) is more common than violence and tends to be under-reported, and — in the unlikely event of arrest — prison practice has been found to lag the country's progressive law.

rewrites.summary:
Iceland is one of the safest countries in the world for transgender visitors. The 2019 Gender Autonomy Act allows self-defined gender registration without diagnosis or surgery, non-binary people can use an 'X' marker, and discrimination on grounds of gender identity and expression is banned in services and employment. General crime rates are very low.

Local travel businesses actively accommodate trans visitors: a dedicated traveller guide reports that most pools in the capital area offer private or gender-neutral changing rooms, that using binary changing rooms is legal and common, and that trans visitors generally 'shouldn't have to be worried about your safety'. Emergency services maintain dedicated guidance for queer victims of abuse and hate crime.

Residual risks are small: potential hate-crime reports have risen in recent years from very low absolute levels, the hate-crime law works through sentencing aggravation rather than a standalone offence, and occasional misgendering — usually unintentional — still occurs.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Policy flux: the 2019 act replaced an earlier registration framework that was itself among the most progressive at the time, and a queer-rights group has called for stronger hate-crime legislation as police-recorded potential hate crimes have climbed (16 in 2023, triple the prior year; 11 in 2024).

rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
Iceland's principal hazards are natural (weather, road conditions, geothermal and volcanic areas) and affect all travellers equally.
